Helical Trajectory

A charged particle with an oblique velocity to a uniform magnetic field follows a helical path. The velocity is naturally split into parallel and perpendicular components.

plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 28: Magnetic Forces and Fields
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional illustration of a positively charged particle following a helical path in a uniform magnetic field. Three axes meet at the origin O, with x running to the right, y upward, and z toward the lower left, and a small orange sphere labeled q sits at the origin. From the particle, a green arrow labeled 'v perp' points straight up along y, a short arrow labeled 'v para' points along the x direction, and a green arrow labeled 'v' between the two gives the total velocity. A blue arrow labeled with a vector B lies along the positive x-axis, and a red arrow labeled 'F' is drawn at the particle. An orange helix of roughly three turns occupies the right side of the frame, each loop circling in the plane perpendicular to x with small arrowheads on the coils marking the sense of rotation, and successive loops shifted steadily in the positive x direction. Above the coils a short green double-headed arrow labeled 'v para' spans the gap between two consecutive turns. Splitting the velocity into two components makes visible which part bends the trajectory and which part carries the particle forward. The drawing shows how a velocity oblique to the field yields circular motion superposed on uniform travel along it.

elements: Coordinate axes (x, y, z) meeting at origin O
Blue arrow for uniform magnetic field 'B' pointing along +x
Orange helical trajectory (3 turns) with directional arrows
Green double-headed pitch annotation bracket labeled 'v_para' above the helix

interactions.teaches: Allows viewing the 3D helical path from different angles to directly observe how circular and linear motions combine.

interactions.label: v_parallel
interactions.teaches: Increasing the parallel velocity stretches the helix pitch. The forward speed determines the spacing between turns, while the gyration radius remains unaffected.

interactions.label: v_perpendicular
interactions.teaches: Increasing the perpendicular velocity expands the helix radius and proportionally increases the magnetic force. The transverse speed governs the gyration without affecting the axial advance per turn.

interactions.label: Play Motion
interactions.teaches: The particle advances continuously along the magnetic field line while simultaneously revolving around it, tracing out a helical path over time.

demo_steps.title: Helical Trajectory
demo_steps.narration: A charged particle with an oblique velocity to a uniform magnetic field follows a helical path. The velocity is naturally split into parallel and perpendicular components.

demo_steps.title: Increase Parallel Velocity
demo_steps.narration: Increasing v_para stretches the helix pitch. The particle covers more distance along the field line during each rotation.

demo_steps.title: Increase Perpendicular Velocity
demo_steps.narration: Increasing v_perp widens the helix radius and strengthens the magnetic force. The particle sweeps a larger circle, but its forward progress per turn is unchanged.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Coordinate system: Origin (0,0,0). Axes extend ±4 units. Particle is an orange sphere (radius 0.15). At initial state t=0, vectors originate at particle: B (blue, length 3, +x), v_para (green, length = vPara, +x), v_perp (green, length = vPerp, +y), v (green, vector sum of v_para and v_perp), F (red, length = vPerp, -z). Helix parameterized by t in [0, 3] (3 full turns): x(t) = vPara * 1.5 * t, y(t) = vPerp * sin(2*pi*t), z(t) = vPerp * (cos(2*pi*t) - 1). Helix is drawn as an orange tube/line with arrowheads. Pitch annotation (green double-headed arrow) sits above the helix from x(1) to x(2) at y = vPerp + 0.4. Colors: particle/helix #e66633, B field #0066cc, velocity #66cc33, force #cc3333.
interactionPlan.notes: Update the helix geometry, pitch annotation length, and vector lengths reactively whenever sliders change. When the animation is active, continuously map time to parameter t from 0 to 3. Move the particle and its attached vectors (v, v_para, v_perp, F) along the helix. Keep v_para aligned with +x. Rotate v_perp dynamically to (0, vPerp*cos(2*pi*t), -vPerp*sin(2*pi*t)) and F to point towards the helix axis at (0, -vPerp*sin(2*pi*t), -vPerp*cos(2*pi*t)). Recompute total v dynamically as v_para + v_perp.

authoredContext:
The result is a helical motion, as shown in the following figure.

A charged particle moving with a velocity not in the same direction as the magnetic field. The velocity component perpendicular to the magnetic field creates circular motion, whereas the component of the velocity parallel to the field moves the particle along a straight line. The pitch is the horizontal distance between two consecutive circles. The resulting motion is helical.

An illustration of a positively charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field. The field is in the positive x direction. The initial velocity is shown as having a component, v sub para, in the positive x direction and another component, v sub perp, in the positive y direction. The particle moves in a helix that loops in the y z plane (counterclockwise from the particle’s perspective) and advances in the positive x direction.

While the charged particle travels in a helical path, it may enter a region where the magnetic field is not uniform. In particular, suppose a particle travels from a region of strong magnetic field to a region of weaker field, then back to a region of stronger field. The particle may reflect back before entering the stronger magnetic field region. This is similar to a wave on a string traveling from a very light, thin string to a hard wall and reflecting backward. If the reflection happens at both ends, the particle is trapped in a so-called magnetic bottle.

A charged particle with an oblique velocity to a uniform magnetic field follows a helical path. The velocity is naturally split into parallel and perpendicular components.

discrepancies: The green shaft of the v_para vector is entirely hidden inside the thicker blue B vector shaft
Vector arrows are rendered much thicker than the standard arrows in the source figure
Vector text labels have misaligned over-arrows that overlap the variable names
The x-axis slopes downward instead of appearing perfectly horizontal on screen
evaluation.notes: Excellent pedagogical interactivity and accurate physics, but visual fidelity suffers from overly thick overlapping arrows and clumsy vector label styling.
action_items: Reduce the shaft and head radii of the custom 3D arrows so they do not swallow each other
Slightly offset or adjust the positioning of B and v_para so both are distinctly visible along the x-axis
Use Unicode combining arrows (e.g., v⃗) or simpler bold styling for vector labels to prevent CSS overlaps
Tweak the camera angle to ensure the x-axis renders perfectly horizontally
